en.title: Kindergarten Counting and Cardinality: Count Sequence
learningGoals: Say the count sequence in order and connect each number word to its written numeral.
Count objects one at a time so that every object gets exactly one number word.
Use the last number said to tell how many objects are in the whole group.
en.launch: Mia lines up six shells on a table and whispers one number word for each shell: one, two, three, four, five, six.
en.conceptExplanation: Counting is a careful matching game. Each object gets exactly one number word, and no object gets counted twice. The last number you say is the size of the whole group. A written numeral is the short mark for that count, so 6 means Mia stopped at six shells.

workedExample.prompt: Mia counts a row of shells one at a time: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. What number tells how many shells there are in all?
workedExample.reasoning: Each shell gets exactly one number word in order, and the last number said is 7. So there are 7 shells, and the numeral 7 records that count.

guidedPractice.prompt: Mia counts a row of shells one at a time: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. What number tells how many shells there are in all?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Point to each shell as you say its number word, then name the last number you said as the total.

independentPractice: Count a group of 8 to 12 classroom objects and write the numeral you land on.
Start at 7 and say the count sequence up to 20 without skipping a number.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Slow down and touch each object as you say its number word, so no number word is left out.
Move or mark each object after you count it, so nothing is counted a second time.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how counting one object at a time helped you tell how many there were.

solutionSteps: Each shell gets exactly one number word in order, and the last number said is 7. So there are 7 shells, and the numeral 7 records that count.

en.title: Kindergarten Counting and Cardinality: Cardinality Compare
learningGoals: Match objects one to one to tell which group has more, fewer, or the same number.
Use the last number said as the number of objects in a group.
Say how many more one group has by counting the leftover objects.
en.launch: Two towers can look different when one is spread out and one is squeezed together, so Jay matches cubes one by one before deciding which group has more.
en.conceptExplanation: Cardinality means the count tells how many are in a group, even if the objects move around. To compare fairly, count both groups or make pairs between them. If one group still has extra unmatched objects, that group has more. If a group runs out first, it has fewer.

workedExample.prompt: There are 6 blue counters and 2 green counters. Which group has more? How many more?
workedExample.answer: The blue group has 4 more counters.
workedExample.reasoning: Match 2 green counters with 2 blue counters. There are 4 blue counters left unmatched, so the blue group has 4 more.

guidedPractice.prompt: There are 5 red counters and 3 yellow counters. Which group has more? How many more?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Match the counters one by one, name the group with unmatched counters, and count the extras.

independentPractice: Build two groups of counters and tell which has more without counting either one.
Make a group with 2 more counters than a group of 6, then check by matching.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: last count word not linked to total
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Count the group again and stop on the last word; say "so there are ___ in all" before answering.
Push the objects into two matching rows before deciding, so the spacing cannot fool your eyes.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how matching one to one helped you tell which group had more.

workedExample.answer: The blue group has 4 more counters.
solutionSteps: Match 2 green counters with 2 blue counters.
Count the 4 blue counters left unmatched.
The blue group has 4 more counters.

en.title: Kindergarten Operations and Algebraic Thinking: Compose Decompose
learningGoals: Show joining and separating within 10 with objects, drawings, or fingers.
Break a number up to 10 into two parts and name both parts.
Write an equation that records the two parts and the whole.
en.launch: Nora has a train of 7 cubes. She breaks it into 4 cubes and 3 cubes, then snaps the parts back together.
en.conceptExplanation: A whole number can be built from parts and broken back into parts. Joining 4 and 3 makes the whole 7, and splitting 7 can reveal 4 and 3 again. Counters, fingers, drawings, and equations can all tell that same within 10 story. The parts may move, but the whole stays connected to them.

workedExample.prompt: Lena has 6 stickers and gets 2 more. How many stickers does Lena have now?
workedExample.reasoning: 6 + 2 = 8, so Lena has 8 stickers. The whole 8 can also be broken into 6 and 2.

guidedPractice.prompt: Lena has 6 stickers and gets 2 more. How many stickers does Lena have now?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Show 6 counters, add 2 more, count the whole group, then write 6 + 2 = 8.

independentPractice: Break 7 into two parts in two different ways and draw each way.
Tell a joining story for 4 + 3 = 7 using classroom objects.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Read the sign aloud before solving: does the story put groups together, or take a part away?
Name the whole and both parts out loud before writing the equation.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how your drawing showed the two parts and the whole.

solutionSteps: 6 + 2 = 8, so Lena has 8 stickers. The whole 8 can also be broken into 6 and 2.

en.title: Kindergarten Number and Operations in Base Ten: Teen Numbers
learningGoals: See a teen number as one full ten and some extra ones.
Fill a ten frame first, then count the leftover counters beside it.
Write a teen number as 10 + ___ so both parts are recorded.
en.launch: A ten-frame bus fills all 10 seats, and 4 more students wait beside it. That picture helps the class see 14.
en.conceptExplanation: Teen numbers are a full ten plus some extra ones. In 14, the 1 means one ten, and the 4 means four ones. Seeing the ten first keeps the number from feeling like a long count of loose objects. Ten and extras makes teen numbers easier to build, read, and write.

workedExample.prompt: A ten-frame is full and 7 more counters are beside it. What teen number is shown?
workedExample.reasoning: One ten and 7 ones make 17.

guidedPractice.prompt: A ten frame is full and 7 more counters are beside it. What teen number is shown?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Say "ten and seven more," then write 10 + 7 = 17.

independentPractice: Build 14 with a full ten frame and extra counters, then write 10 + 4 = 14.
Show 18 two ways: with counters and with the numeral.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Point to the ten frame first: in 17 the 1 stands for one whole ten, not one single counter.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how the full ten frame helped you name the teen number.

solutionSteps: One ten and 7 ones make 17.

en.title: Kindergarten Measurement and Data: Attributes Data
learningGoals: Describe an object by a measurable attribute such as length or weight.
Compare two objects directly and say which is longer, shorter, heavier, or lighter.
Sort objects into categories and count how many are in each category.
en.launch: At the art table, a pencil is longer than an eraser, but the eraser feels heavier in your hand.
en.conceptExplanation: Measurement starts by choosing one attribute to notice. Length, height, weight, and color answer different questions, so you compare only one kind of thing at a time. Measuring works best when the same unit or rule is used for every object. Then your data tells a fair story about what is longer, heavier, taller, or shorter.

workedExample.prompt: Line a pencil and a crayon up at the same edge of the table. The pencil reaches past the end of the crayon. Which object is longer?
workedExample.reasoning: Both start at the same edge, so the one that reaches further is longer. The pencil reaches past the crayon, so the pencil is longer.

guidedPractice.prompt: Line a pencil and a crayon up at the same edge of the table. The pencil reaches past the end of the crayon. Which object is longer?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Line both objects up at the same starting point, look at which one reaches further, and name it as the longer one.

independentPractice: Find two classroom objects and tell which is longer and how you know.
Sort a handful of blocks by color, then sort the same blocks again by size.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Ask which object reaches further from the shared starting line, not how many objects are on the table.
Sort the same objects a second time by a different attribute, such as size instead of color.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how you compared the two objects and what you found.

solutionSteps: 11 is greater than 8, so the pencil is longer.

en.title: Kindergarten Geometry: Shapes Position
learningGoals: Use position words such as above, below, beside, and next to.
Name flat and solid shapes and tell how many sides or corners they have.
Put shapes together to build a larger shape.
en.launch: A paper triangle is still a triangle when you turn it sideways, slide it under a book, or color it green.
en.conceptExplanation: A shape gets its name from its attributes. A triangle has three straight sides, and a rectangle has four square corners, no matter which way it faces. Position words tell where the shape is, not what the shape is. Words like above, below, beside, and inside help you describe the scene clearly.

workedExample.prompt: Which shape has 3 straight sides?
workedExample.reasoning: A triangle has 3 straight sides.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which shape has 3 straight sides?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Count the straight sides on each shape, then name the one with exactly 3.

independentPractice: Name three objects in the room and describe where each one is using a position word.
Use two triangles to build a larger shape and name what you made.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Turn the shape or stretch it: a triangle is still a triangle with 3 straight sides in any position.
Ask whether the shape is flat like a drawing or solid like a block before naming it.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how you knew which shape was which.

solutionSteps: A triangle has 3 straight sides.

en.title: Grade 1 Operations and Algebraic Thinking: Add Subtract
learningGoals: Solve addition and subtraction word problems within 20.
Use the commutative and associative properties to make a problem easier.
Build fluency by counting on, making ten, and using facts you already know.
en.launch: Lena has 8 blue stickers on her desk, then a friend gives her 3 green stickers. She draws the desk before writing any numbers so each number has a job in the story.
en.conceptExplanation: Addition is the story of parts joining to make a whole, so Lena can show 8 + 3 = 11. Subtraction is the story of a whole changing, being compared, or being split to find a missing part. The equals sign means both sides have the same value, so 11 = 8 + 3 is true too. Counters, ten-frames, number lines, and equations are different ways to prove the answer fits within 20.

workedExample.prompt: Lena has 7 stickers and gets 4 more. How many stickers does Lena have now?
workedExample.reasoning: 7 + 4 = 11, so Lena has 11 stickers. The equation 11 = 7 + 4 is also true because both sides have the same value.

guidedPractice.prompt: Lena has 7 stickers and gets 4 more. How many stickers does Lena have now?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Count on 4 from 7, or make ten (7 + 3 = 10, then 10 + 1), then check that 11 fits the story.

independentPractice: Write your own joining story for 8 + 5 and solve it two different ways.
Find the missing number in 6 + ___ = 13 and explain your strategy.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Retell the story in your own words and act it out; the action, not a keyword, decides the operation.
Read = as "is the same amount as" and check that both sides name the same number.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain which strategy you used and why it worked.

solutionSteps: 7 + 4 = 11, so Lena has 11 stickers. The equation 11 = 7 + 4 is also true because both sides have the same value.

en.title: Grade 1 Number and Operations in Base Ten: Place Value
learningGoals: Count, read, and write numbers to 120.
Show a two-digit number as a number of tens and a number of ones.
Compare two-digit numbers with >, =, and < by comparing the tens first.
en.launch: The classroom library has 5 bundles of ten bookmarks and 4 single bookmarks waiting in a cup.
en.conceptExplanation: Place value tells what a digit is worth because of where it sits. In 54, the 5 means five tens, and the 4 means four ones. Bundles keep the tens from getting mixed with loose ones. When you compare, add, or subtract two-digit numbers, keep tens with tens and ones with ones so the story stays organized.

workedExample.prompt: A number has 6 tens and 2 ones. What is the number?
workedExample.reasoning: 6 tens and 2 ones make 62.

guidedPractice.prompt: A number has 6 tens and 2 ones. What is the number?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Build 6 tens and 2 ones, say "sixty-two," and write 62.

independentPractice: Build 45 with tens and ones, then show the same number a different way.
Compare 38 and 83 and explain which is greater using tens and ones.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Say what each digit is worth: in 62 the 6 means 6 tens, or 60, not 6.
Regroup one ten into ten ones instead of flipping the digits around.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how tens and ones helped you name or compare the number.

solutionSteps: 6 tens and 2 ones make 62.

en.title: Grade 1 Measurement and Data: Measure Data
learningGoals: Order three objects by length and compare two objects using a third one.
Measure length by laying same-size units end to end with no gaps or overlaps.
Read a picture or bar graph and answer how many more or how many fewer.
en.launch: Sofia measures a ribbon with paper clips. If the clips overlap or leave gaps, the ribbon seems to change length even though it did not move.
en.conceptExplanation: A measurement number needs both a unit and an object. Length tells how long something is, and a fair measure repeats the same unit from end to end. You can compare two lengths, count spaces on a ruler or number line, and sort data to answer questions. The label tells what the number is counting.

workedExample.prompt: A ribbon is 13 units long. A string is 8 units long. How many units longer is the ribbon?
workedExample.reasoning: 13 - 8 = 5, so the ribbon is 5 units longer.

guidedPractice.prompt: A ribbon is 13 units long. A string is 8 units long. How many units longer is the ribbon?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Line both lengths up at the same starting point, then subtract: 13 - 8 = 5 units longer.

independentPractice: Measure a pencil with paper clips and record the length in units.
Make a picture graph of three snack choices and say which had the most.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Lay the units end to end and touching, with no space between them and none on top of another.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: counting tick marks instead of intervals
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Count the spaces between the marks, not the marks themselves — the spaces are the units.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how you measured or compared, and what unit you used.

solutionSteps: 13 - 8 = 5, so the ribbon is 5 units longer.

en.title: Grade 1 Geometry: Shape Reasoning
learningGoals: Tell defining attributes, such as number of sides, apart from non-defining ones, such as color.
Combine two or more shapes to make a new shape.
Split a circle or rectangle into halves and fourths and name the equal shares.
en.launch: A folded paper napkin can become two equal shares, but only if both pieces are the same size.
en.conceptExplanation: Shape reasoning begins with attributes that must be true. A rectangle stays a rectangle when it is big, small, tilted, or blue because it still has the needed sides and square corners. Equal shares are about fairness: each part must match in size. That is when words like halves and fourths make sense.

workedExample.prompt: A rectangle is split into 2 equal shares. What are the shares called?
workedExample.reasoning: Two equal shares of one whole are called halves.

guidedPractice.prompt: A rectangle is split into 2 equal shares. What are the shares called?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Check that both shares are exactly the same size, then name each one a half.

independentPractice: Fold a paper rectangle into fourths and name one share.
Build a rectangle out of two squares and describe the new shape.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Sort by sides and corners first; color and size do not decide what a shape is.
Compare the pieces: shares are halves only when they are exactly the same size.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain what made the shares equal.

solutionSteps: Two equal shares of one whole are called halves.

en.title: Grade 2 Operations and Algebraic Thinking: Fluency Arrays
learningGoals: Solve one- and two-step addition and subtraction word problems within 100.
Add and subtract within 20 fluently using mental strategies.
Show equal groups as an array and write a repeated addition equation.
en.launch: At snack time, plates are set in rows. Some stories ask how many snacks are added, and some ask how many are in equal rows.
en.conceptExplanation: Addition and subtraction tell change, comparison, and part-whole stories. Arrays show equal groups because every row or column has the same amount. Fluency means you can choose a strategy that fits the story, not just rush to an answer. A quick check asks whether the equation matches the picture, rows, or words.

workedExample.prompt: 4 teams each collect 4 stickers. How many stickers do the teams collect altogether?
workedExample.reasoning: Each team is an equal group of 4 stickers. Add the 4 equal groups: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 stickers.

guidedPractice.prompt: 4 teams each collect 4 stickers. How many stickers do the teams collect altogether?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Draw 4 rows of 4, add 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16, and label the answer with stickers.

independentPractice: Write a two-step problem for a classmate, then solve it yourself first.
Draw an array for 3 rows of 5 and write the repeated addition equation.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Underline every question in the problem; a two-step problem is not finished until the last question is answered.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: even/odd judged by last spoken number only
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Pair the objects up: a number is even only when nothing is left over.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how your array or equation matched the story.

solutionSteps: Each team is an equal group of 4 stickers. Add the 4 equal groups: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 stickers.

en.title: Grade 2 Number and Operations in Base Ten: Three Digit Place Value
learningGoals: Read, write, and build three-digit numbers as hundreds, tens, and ones.
Compare three-digit numbers by comparing hundreds first, then tens, then ones.
Add and subtract within 1000, regrouping when a place is full or short.
en.launch: A school store records 145 pencils as 1 full box of hundreds, 4 packs of tens, and 5 loose pencils.
en.conceptExplanation: Three-digit place value is a packing system for hundreds, tens, and ones. In 145, each digit names a different kind of unit. Regrouping is a trade, such as 10 ones for 1 ten or 10 tens for 1 hundred, without changing the total. Line up matching places so hundreds talk to hundreds, tens to tens, and ones to ones.

workedExample.prompt: A number has 2 hundreds, 3 tens, and 6 ones. What is the number?
workedExample.reasoning: 2 hundreds, 3 tens, and 6 ones make 236.

guidedPractice.prompt: A number has 2 hundreds, 3 tens, and 6 ones. What is the number?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Build 2 hundreds, 3 tens, and 6 ones, say "two hundred thirty-six," and write 236.

independentPractice: Build 405 with base-ten blocks and explain the zero in the tens place.
Add 268 + 147 and show where you regrouped.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Trade a real bundle: 10 ones become 1 ten and 10 tens become 1 hundred, so the total never changes.
Line the numbers up by place value, not by the right edge of the page, before you add.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain what each digit was worth in the number you worked with.

solutionSteps: 2 hundreds, 3 tens, and 6 ones make 236.

en.title: Grade 2 Measurement and Data: Measure Data Money Time
learningGoals: Measure and estimate lengths with rulers and standard units.
Show lengths and length differences on a number line.
Tell time to five minutes and count coin values to solve money problems.
en.launch: Field day has jump distances, coin collections, clock times, and class votes. The numbers only make sense when their units come along.
en.conceptExplanation: A unit tells what kind of quantity a number describes. Length can be shown on a number line, money is counted by coin values, time uses hours and minutes, and data displays help compare answers. Keeping the unit with the number stops mix-ups. Then you know whether to count, add, subtract, or read from a graph.

workedExample.prompt: A ribbon is 14 units long. A string is 8 units long. How many units longer is the ribbon?
workedExample.reasoning: 14 - 8 = 6, so the ribbon is 6 units longer.

guidedPractice.prompt: A ribbon is 14 units long. A string is 8 units long. How many units longer is the ribbon?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Show both lengths on a number line, find the gap between them, and write 14 - 8 = 6 units.

independentPractice: Measure two objects in centimeters and record the difference.
Count a set of coins two different ways and check that both totals match.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Convert both measurements to the same unit before comparing or subtracting.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: coin value counted as coin count
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Count by each coin's value — three dimes is 30 cents, not 3 cents.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain which unit you used and why it fit the problem.

solutionSteps: 14 - 8 = 6, so the ribbon is 6 units longer.

en.title: Grade 2 Geometry: Partition Shapes
learningGoals: Recognize and draw shapes by their number of sides, angles, and faces.
Split a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count them.
Partition circles and rectangles into halves, thirds, and fourths.
en.launch: Ava cuts a brownie pan for friends and also arranges square tiles in neat rows and columns.
en.conceptExplanation: Partitioning means splitting one whole into equal shares. Halves, thirds, and fourths name how many equal pieces fill the whole, not how big the drawing looks. Rows and columns are another equal-size structure. When rectangles are tiled evenly, you can count groups instead of counting every square one at a time.

workedExample.prompt: Which shape name matches a polygon with 4 sides?
workedExample.reasoning: A polygon with 4 sides is a quadrilateral.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which shape name matches a polygon with 4 sides?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Count the sides on each choice and name the four-sided one a quadrilateral.

independentPractice: Draw a rectangle split into 3 rows of 4 squares and count the total.
Split a circle into fourths and name one share two different ways.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Check that every share is the same size; unequal pieces are not thirds or fourths.
Say the rows first and then the columns, and check that the drawing matches the words.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how you knew the shares were equal.

solutionSteps: A polygon with 4 sides is a quadrilateral.

en.title: Grade 3 Operations and Algebraic Thinking: Mult Div
learningGoals: Interpret products and quotients as equal groups, arrays, or area.
Solve multiplication and division word problems within 100.
Use properties and patterns to find facts you do not yet know by heart.
en.launch: A garden has equal rows of seedlings. Once you know what one row means, the whole garden becomes easier to describe.
en.conceptExplanation: Multiplication is a shortcut for equal groups that repeat. Division reverses the story by asking how many groups there are or how many items are in each group. Arrays, skip-counting, number lines, and related facts all show the same equal groups idea. The equation should match the group size, number of groups, and total.

workedExample.prompt: 5 teams each collect 4 stickers. How many stickers do the teams collect altogether?
workedExample.reasoning: 5 equal groups of 4 make 5 × 4 = 20.

guidedPractice.prompt: 5 teams each collect 4 stickers. How many stickers do the teams collect altogether?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Read it as 5 groups of 4, write 5 × 4 = 20, and label the answer with stickers.

independentPractice: Write a division story that matches 24 ÷ 6 and solve it.
Use 5 × 7 = 35 to find 6 × 7, and explain the step.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Also show the fact as an array or an area model, so 5 × 4 and 4 × 5 both make sense.
Decide first whether the story shares into a known number of groups, or makes groups of a known size.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how your model showed the groups in the story.

solutionSteps: 5 equal groups of 4 make 5 × 4 = 20.

en.title: Grade 3 Number and Operations in Base Ten: Arithmetic
learningGoals: Round whole numbers to the nearest 10 or 100.
Add and subtract within 1000 using place-value strategies.
Multiply one-digit numbers by multiples of 10.
en.launch: A ticket counter has hundreds, tens, and ones windows. The clerk estimates first so the final count has a sensible size.
en.conceptExplanation: Rounding uses place value to choose a nearby friendly number. Multi-digit addition, subtraction, and multiplication work because each digit keeps its own place. Hundreds combine with hundreds, tens with tens, and ones with ones. An estimate is like a reasonableness spotlight: it helps catch answers that are far too large or too small.

workedExample.reasoning: Add by place value: 200 + 100 = 300, 40 + 30 = 70, and 6 + 0 = 6. Combine the parts: 300 + 70 + 6 = 376.

guidedPractice.expectedMove: Add hundreds to hundreds and tens to tens: 200 + 100 = 300 and 46 + 30 = 76, so the sum is 376.

independentPractice: Round 372 to the nearest ten and to the nearest hundred, and explain the difference.
Find 8 × 60 and explain the place-value step.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: rounding to nearest digit not place

en.title: Grade 3 Number and Operations - Fractions: Fraction Meaning
learningGoals: Understand a fraction as a number of equal parts of one whole.
Locate fractions on a number line and compare them to 0, 1, and each other.
Compare fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator.
en.launch: A class shares same-size granola bars and marks the pieces on a number line so the pieces become numbers, not just snacks.

The whole must stay the same size when fractions are compared. On a number line, equivalent fractions land on the same point even if their names look different.

Draw two fraction strips that show why 2/6 and 1/3 are equal.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Compare the size of one part: a larger denominator cuts the same whole into smaller pieces.
Draw both fractions on wholes of the same size before comparing them.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain what the denominator told you about the size of each part.

solutionSteps: For unit fractions, the smaller denominator makes the larger piece, so 1/4 is greater than 1/5.

en.title: Grade 3 Measurement and Data: Time Data Area Perimeter

en.launch: A park map shows a garden bed, a walking path around it, a clock for the visit, and a chart of favorite flowers.

workedExample.reasoning: Area is length × width, so 12 × 3 = 36 square units.

guidedPractice.prompt: A rectangle is 12 units long and 3 units wide. What is its area?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Multiply length by width: 12 × 3 = 36, and label the answer in square units.

independentPractice: Draw two different rectangles that each have an area of 24 square units.
Find the perimeter of a 12-by-3 rectangle and explain how it differs from the area.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Ask what is being measured: area covers the inside in square units, perimeter walks the border in length units.
Read the key or the scale first — one symbol or one grid line may stand for more than one.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain what your answer measured and what unit it used.

solutionSteps: Area is length × width, so 12 × 3 = 36 square units.

en.title: Grade 3 Geometry: Categories
learningGoals: Sort shapes into categories by shared attributes such as having four sides.
Explain why one shape can belong to more than one category.
Split a shape into equal parts and name one part as a unit fraction of the area.
en.launch: In a shape museum, one quadrilateral can wear more than one label if it has all the needed properties.
en.conceptExplanation: Polygons are classified by sides, angles, and special properties. A quadrilateral has four sides, and some quadrilaterals are also rectangles, rhombuses, or squares. Categories can overlap because one shape may satisfy several rules at once. When a shape is split into equal areas, the fraction name depends on equal parts of the same whole.

workedExample.reasoning: The 4 parts have equal area, so 1 part is 1 out of 4 equal parts of the whole. That area is 1/4 of the rectangle.

guidedPractice.prompt: A rectangle is divided into 4 equal parts. What fraction of the whole area is 1 part?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Check that the 4 parts are equal, then name one part 1/4 of the whole area.

independentPractice: Name a shape that is both a rectangle and a rhombus, and explain why.
Split a shape into 6 equal parts and name the area of two parts together.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Check every attribute; a square meets the rules for rectangle and rhombus at the same time.
Measure or fold to confirm the parts are the same size before naming a unit fraction.

solutionSteps: The 4 parts have equal area, so 1 part is 1 out of 4 equal parts of the whole. That area is 1/4 of the rectangle.

en.title: Grade 4 Operations and Algebraic Thinking: Factors Patterns
learningGoals: Interpret multiplication as a comparison, such as 3 times as many.

en.launch: A bracelet maker counts beads in repeated groups and notices that some group sizes build the total exactly.
en.conceptExplanation: Multiplicative comparison tells how many times as many, while additive comparison tells how many more. Factors are numbers that make a product exactly, and multiples are products of a number. Patterns can reveal a hidden rule across steps. In multi-step problems, each equation should answer one part of the situation before the next step begins.

workedExample.prompt: Which number is a factor of 24: 5, 6, or 7?
workedExample.reasoning: 6 is a factor of 24 because 6 × 4 = 24.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which number is a factor of 24: 5, 6, or 7?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Test each one by dividing: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 with no remainder, so 6 is a factor.

independentPractice: List every factor pair of 36 and say whether 36 is prime or composite.
Write a rule for the pattern 3, 7, 11, 15 and extend it two more terms.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: additive comparison used for multiplicative comparison
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Ask whether the story says "how many more" (subtract) or "times as many" (multiply).
A factor divides the number; a multiple is built from it — test both with 6 and 24 before answering.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how you checked that your answer was reasonable.

solutionSteps: 6 is a factor of 24 because 6 × 4 = 24.

en.title: Grade 4 Number and Operations in Base Ten: Multi Digit
learningGoals: Explain that a digit in one place is worth ten times the same digit one place to its right.
Multiply up to four-digit numbers by one-digit numbers.
Divide multi-digit numbers by one-digit divisors and interpret the remainder.
en.launch: A city counter reads 34,628 visitors. Each digit has a place, and each place is ten times the place to its right.
en.conceptExplanation: Place value is the engine for multi-digit numbers. It helps you read, compare, round, add, subtract, multiply, and divide because every digit carries a unit. Moving one place left makes a value ten times as large; moving right makes it one tenth as large. Algorithms make sense when you can explain the trades behind them.

workedExample.prompt: Multiply 34 × 7.
workedExample.reasoning: Break 34 into 30 and 4. Multiply each part by 7: 30 × 7 = 210 and 4 × 7 = 28. Add the partial products: 210 + 28 = 238.

guidedPractice.prompt: Multiply 34 × 7.
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Break 34 into 30 + 4, multiply each part (210 and 28), then add: 238.

independentPractice: Find 34 × 26 with an area model and with the standard algorithm, then compare the two.
Divide 87 by 5 and explain what the remainder means in a sharing story.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Explain the shift as multiplying by 10, not as a trick of writing an extra zero.
Return to the story: the remainder may be dropped, shared, or rounded up depending on what is asked.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how place value guided your calculation.

solutionSteps: Break 34 into 30 and 4. Multiply each part by 7: 30 × 7 = 210 and 4 × 7 = 28. Add the partial products: 210 + 28 = 238.

en.title: Grade 4 Number and Operations - Fractions: Fraction Decimal
learningGoals: Generate equivalent fractions and compare fractions with unlike denominators.

en.launch: Two measuring cups can hold the same amount even when one is marked in fractions and the other is marked in decimals.
en.conceptExplanation: Equivalent fractions name the same quantity with different-sized pieces. To add or subtract fractions, the pieces must be the same unit fraction first. Decimals also use place value, so tenths line up with tenths and hundredths with hundredths. Models, number lines, and equations should all point to the same quantity.

guidedPractice.prompt: Mia shades 2/6 of a strip and then shades 2/6 more. What fraction is shaded?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: The parts are the same size, so add the numerators: 2/6 + 2/6 = 4/6, which is also 2/3.

independentPractice: Show with a drawing why 3/4 and 6/8 are equivalent.
Write 0.7 and 0.70 as fractions and explain why they are equal.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: With the same numerator, the larger denominator gives the smaller fraction — check it with a drawing.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Compare place by place: 0.7 is greater than 0.65 because 7 tenths beats 6 tenths.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how you knew the two fractions could be combined or compared.

solutionSteps: The denominators match, so add the numerators: 2/6 + 2/6 = 4/6.

solutionSteps: Add the angle measures: 50° + 32° = 82°.

en.title: Grade 4 Geometry: Lines Shapes
learningGoals: Draw and identify points, lines, rays, angles, and parallel and perpendicular lines.

en.launch: On a map, some streets never meet, some cross in square corners, and a folded design has two matching halves.
en.conceptExplanation: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart, and perpendicular lines meet at right angles. An angle measures the amount of turn, not the length of the rays. workedExample.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
workedExample.reasoning: A line of symmetry folds a figure into two matching halves. A square matches when folded along each diagonal and along each line through the midpoints of opposite sides, giving 4 lines of symmetry.

guidedPractice.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Fold the square along each possible line; 4 folds match exactly, so a square has 4 lines of symmetry.

independentPractice: Draw a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides and name it.
Find the lines of symmetry in a rectangle that is not a square.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Test with a ruler or a square corner: parallel lines never meet, and perpendicular lines form a right angle at any tilt.
Fold the figure, or trace and flip it, to confirm both halves match exactly.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain the property you used to classify or to fold the figure.

solutionSteps: A line of symmetry folds a figure into two matching halves. A square matches when folded along each diagonal and along each line through the midpoints of opposite sides, giving 4 lines of symmetry.

en.title: Grade 5 Operations and Algebraic Thinking: Expressions Patterns
learningGoals: Write and evaluate numerical expressions that use parentheses and brackets.

en.launch: A game machine gives points by following a rule. Parentheses on the score card tell which part of the rule happens first.
en.conceptExplanation: A numerical expression is a plan for calculations, not just an answer waiting at the end. The order of operations tells how to read that plan: grouping symbols first, then multiplication or division, then addition or subtraction. workedExample.reasoning: First add inside the parentheses: 7 + 2 = 9. Then multiply: 9 × 4 = 36.

guidedPractice.expectedMove: Do the work inside the parentheses first: 7 + 2 = 9, then 9 × 4 = 36.

independentPractice: Write an expression for "twice the sum of 6 and 4" and evaluate it.
Generate an "add 3" pattern and an "add 6" pattern from 0, and describe how the terms relate.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: order of operations as left-to-right only
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Work the grouping symbols first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract.

commonPitfalls.pitfall: pattern rule inferred from one pair
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Test the rule on at least three terms before you trust it.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain the order you worked in and why it mattered.

solutionSteps: First add inside the parentheses: 7 + 2 = 9. Then multiply: 9 × 4 = 36.

en.title: Grade 5 Number and Operations in Base Ten: Decimals
learningGoals: Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths using place value.

en.launch: A science scale shows 3.248 grams. The decimal point is the doorway between whole units and smaller parts of one unit.
en.conceptExplanation: Decimals extend place value to tenths, hundredths, and thousandths. Each place is one tenth of the place to its left, so alignment matters when you compare or compute. workedExample.reasoning: Align decimal place values: 5.4 + 1.2 = 6.6.

guidedPractice.prompt: What is 5.4 + 1.2?

independentPractice: Compare 0.305 and 0.35 and explain which is greater.
Find 2.5 × 10 and 2.5 ÷ 10, and describe how the digits shift.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Multiplying by 10 moves each digit one place to the left (larger); dividing moves it one place to the right (smaller).

commonPitfalls.pitfall: aligning digits instead of place values
commonPitfalls.repairMove: Line up the decimal points, not the last digits, before adding or subtracting.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how place value kept your decimal answer correct.

solutionSteps: Align decimal place values: 5.4 + 1.2 = 6.6.

en.title: Grade 5 Number and Operations - Fractions: Operations
learningGoals: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by first finding a common denominator.

en.launch: A recipe card asks for fractional cups of oats and sugar. The cook first asks what one whole cup means.
en.conceptExplanation: Unlike fractions need common units before they can be added or subtracted. Multiplying by a fraction can mean taking part of a quantity, like half of a batch. guidedPractice.expectedMove: Rewrite 1/2 as 2/4 so the parts match, then add: 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4 mile.

independentPractice: Find 2/3 × 3/5 and draw an area model that shows the product.
Write a story for 4 divided by 1/2 and explain why the answer is greater than 4.

solutionSteps: Rename 1/2 as 2/4, then add 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4.

en.title: Grade 5 Measurement and Data: Volume Data
learningGoals: Convert among units within one measurement system and use the conversion to solve problems.

Find volume by counting unit cubes and by using length × width × height.
en.launch: A display box is filled with unit cubes, layer by layer, until the inside space is packed without gaps.
en.conceptExplanation: Volume counts cubic units inside a solid figure, not square units on its surface. guidedPractice.prompt: A rectangular prism is 8 units long, 4 units wide, and 2 units high. What is its volume?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Multiply the three dimensions: 8 × 4 × 2 = 64, and label the answer in cubic units.

independentPractice: Build two different prisms that each have a volume of 24 cubic units, and record their dimensions.

commonPitfalls.repairMove: Count the cubes in one layer, then check that length × width gives the same layer count.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain what your answer measured and the unit it used.

solutionSteps: Volume is length × width × height, so 8 × 4 × 2 = 64 cubic units.

en.title: Grade 5 Geometry: Coordinate Shapes
learningGoals: Plot and name points in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane.

en.launch: A treasure map uses an ordered pair to tell you where to go: move across first, then move up.
en.conceptExplanation: An ordered pair (x, y) gives directions from the origin. The x-axis move is horizontal, and the y-axis move is vertical. guidedPractice.prompt: Point A is 6 steps right from the origin and 7 steps up. What ordered pair names point A?
guidedPractice.expectedMove: Write the horizontal move first, then the vertical move: (6, 7).

independentPractice: Plot (3, 5) and (5, 3) and explain why they are different points.
Explain why every square is a rectangle but not every rectangle is a square.

Check the properties in order: a figure keeps every property of the category above it.

en.exitTicket: In one sentence, explain how the order of the coordinates, or the properties, decided your answer.

solutionSteps: The first coordinate is the horizontal move and the second coordinate is the vertical move, so A is (6, 7).
